title: Platform APIs
summary: OAuth grants, client credentials limits, region hosts, and why this lab’s explorer never sends a request.

lessons.title: The Developer Center is the map. This lab is not a client.
lessons.summary: It is the front door for the Platform API. Read the public docs. Do not point a tutorial at a production org.
paras: The Genesys Cloud Developer Center is the front door for the Platform API. The API explorer in this lab shows sample JSON shaped from the client-credentials guide and from admin limits such as queue alerting. It does not call login or API hosts. A sample with labIllustration set to true is a teaching body, not a captured response.

When you do build a client, the region’s login host and API host must match the organization. This lab treats only the US East API host from the client-credentials guide, api.mypurecloud.com, as a host it is willing to print. Other regions: confirm the API host on the regions article.

lessons.title: Pick the grant that matches who the call runs as
lessons.summary: Client credentials, authorization code with PKCE, and SAML2 Bearer are the grants to learn. Implicit is the one leaving.
paras: The create-an-OAuth-client article lists the grant types you can assign. Client credentials are for a service. Authorization code, with PKCE where the article requires it, is for an application that acts as a user. SAML2 Bearer is the enterprise single-sign-on pattern the article includes. Token Implicit Grant is documented as deprecated after 25 May 2026.
A grant is not a role. After you pick the grant you still assign role and division pairs. A correct grant with an empty role list returns a token that cannot see the queues you meant.

figure.caption: Grant first, then roles and divisions.

lessons.title: Client credentials have no user, so users/me is the wrong call
lessons.summary: The token is the client. The guide shows that limit on purpose.
paras: The client-credentials guide shows a POST to the login host’s /oauth/token with HTTP Basic of the client id and secret, and grant_type=client_credentials. The access token is then a bearer token against the API host. The same guide explains that this token cannot call /api/v2/users/me, because there is no user.

Roles on a client-credentials client are role-and-division pairs, and they are a subset of what the person who created the client could grant. You cannot escalate by creating a client. If the integration must read “my” queues, use authorization code instead.

figure.caption: Basic auth at login. Bearer at the API. No user on the token.

lessons.title: Implicit grant is a migration, not a new design
lessons.summary: The OAuth article dates the deprecation: after 25 May 2026.
paras: Token Implicit Grant returns a token in the browser redirect. That pattern is what the create-an-OAuth-client article marks deprecated after 25 May 2026. New work uses authorization code with PKCE, or client credentials when there is no user. Leaving an implicit client in place is a dated risk, not a style choice.
Inventory the clients before the date. Each one is either a user-facing app or a service. Split them. Do not “fix” an implicit app by pasting its token into a data action.
lessons.uncertainty: Confirm the deprecation sentence on the OAuth article before you enforce 25 May 2026 in a program plan.

figure.caption: Implicit clients move to code+PKCE or to client credentials.

lessons.title: Login host and API host are a pair you look up
lessons.summary: US East is the pair this lab will quote in full. Other rows stay on the regions article.
paras: US East (N. Virginia, us-east-1) uses login.mypurecloud.com and, in the client-credentials guide, api.mypurecloud.com. US West (Oregon, us-west-2) uses login.usw2.pure.cloud. FedRAMP (US East 2, us-east-2) uses login.use2.us-gov-pure.cloud. This lab does not invent the API hostname that pairs with those last two logins.
A token from one region’s login host is not a token for another region’s API. Satellite regions do not change this. They are media. The organization still has one core region and one login.

lessons.title: Role and division pairs are the real permission
lessons.summary: A token opens the door the role allows, in the division the pair names.
paras: Divisions overview: objects live in one division, Home cannot be deleted, and the All division is the org-wide grant. OAuth clients do not escape that model. The client-credentials article’s role-division pairs are how a service is scoped. Granting a queue role in Home does not let the client edit a queue that lives in another division.

Transactional objects such as conversations and recordings follow the division rules on that page. An integration that “cannot see the recording” is often a division grant, not a broken endpoint. Check the pair before you file an API defect.

figure.caption: The same role in two divisions is two grants.

lessons.title: SCIM and other directory sync still start with an OAuth client
lessons.summary: The OAuth article points SCIM at a client. The client still has roles and a grant.
paras: Create an OAuth client is the article that tells you SCIM uses an OAuth client. Treat that client like any other service: a deliberate grant, least roles, a division pair, a secret that is not in a ticket. Directory sync that can create users can also create admins if the role is wide.

SCIM does not choose your region, your queues, or your bots. After users exist, the org work in the other tracks still has to happen. A synced user with no queue membership and Off Queue is a successful SCIM call and an empty contact center.
